newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Britain at odds over Zaire at summit.
newsitem.headline: France, Britain at odds over Zaire at summit.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac looked set to fail to persuade British Prime Minister John Major on Friday to send troops to Zaire as part of a multi-national force to protect refugees threatened by war.

Both leaders, at a two-day meeting in Bordeaux ending on Friday, expressed deep concerns over a humanitarian disaster that has left 1.2 million Hutu refugees with little water or food after an uprising by Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire.
But France and Britain, which have a long history of close military cooperation including in Bosnia and the 1991 U.S.-led Gulf War against Iraq, disagreed on what to do.

"The aim is to reach...a common humanitarian, diplomatic and political position with Britain on Zaire," Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna told reporters after the two leaders met over dinner in a restaurant in the southwestern city of Bordeaux.

A senior British official all but ruled out sending troops to Zaire as part of a international force of 5,000 troops proposed by France and Spain. "We're just not at that sort of point at the moment," he told reporters.

He said Zaire was a complex tangle of problems in a part of Africa where he said many nations had interests. He also said that only one part of France's proposals involved sending troops. "It isn't a precise military plan," he added.

France and Spain ended isolated at a meeting of European Union development ministers in Brussels on Thursday in urging military force despite charges by French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette that the world was being "spineless" over Zaire.
At the United Nations, France proposed that the U.N. Security Council should approve an intervention force for two months.

In one military accord between France and Britain, defence ministers were to sign a deal in Bordeaux on Friday to bolster naval cooperation in areas including logistical support, training and arms procurement programmes.

"It has long been recognised by both countries that the Royal Navy and the French navy are very similar in size, shape, strategic role and outlook," British Defence Minister Michael Portillo said in a statement.

"This will be a very dynamic and active initiative between the two foremost European navies. It will build on the already impressive depth and range of bilateral defence cooperation which exists between Britain and France."
Colonna said Chirac and Major devoted almost an hour at a dinner she described as relaxed and calm to discussing EU plans for economic and monetary union from 1999.
"Each side remained on its known positions," she said. France would like Britain to join a single EU currency but the British government has yet to decide whether to do so.
Major told Chirac that Britain was sticking to its commitments to eradicate mad cow disease with the slaughter of more than 750,000 cattle so far.
France led an international ban on imports of British beef in March after evidence that the fatal brain disease could spread to humans.
